scenes.text: On a hot day when you haven't had much to drink, you pass a small amount of dark yellow urine. Drink a litre of water quickly, and within an hour or so you pass a lot of pale urine. Same kidneys, same day, opposite results. The colour is a clue: similar wastes dissolved in less water, or in more. So what tells your kidneys how much water to keep, and how do they do it?

The variable here isn't how much you drink. It's how concentrated your blood is: how much dissolved salt and other particles there are in each litre of blood plasma. Biologists call this osmolarity. Lose water by sweating or breathing out, and the same particles sit in less water, so osmolarity rises. Drink lots of water, and osmolarity falls. Remember osmosis from Year 11: water moves across a membrane towards the side with more dissolved particles. That rule explains most of this video.

Your kidneys control how much water leaves. Each kidney holds about a million tiny tubes called nephrons. At the start of each one, blood is filtered, and water and small particles are pushed into the tube. This fluid, the filtrate, then flows along the tubule, and most of it is taken back into the blood. That's reabsorption. Filtering isn't choosy about water, so control comes from what's taken back. Here's the surprise: your kidneys filter around a hundred and eighty litres a day, yet you pass only about one and a half. The last stretch, the collecting duct, sets how much of the rest you keep.

So who's measuring? In the hypothalamus are osmoreceptors, cells that sense blood concentration. When blood gets too concentrated, water leaves them by osmosis and they shrink slightly. That's the detection. The hypothalamus then sends nerve impulses down to the posterior pituitary, the back part of a small gland just below it. The pituitary releases ADH, antidiuretic hormone, into the blood. ADH is made in the hypothalamus, but it's stored in and released from the pituitary. So one step is neural, and the next is hormonal. The hypothalamus also makes you thirsty, because your kidneys can save water, but only drinking replaces it.

ADH travels in the blood to the collecting ducts. There, it binds to the duct cells and moves water channels, called aquaporins, from inside the cells into the membrane facing the filtrate. The tissue around the ducts is very concentrated, so once the channels are in, water moves out of the duct by osmosis and back into the blood. Less water is left in the duct, so you make a smaller volume of more concentrated urine.

As water returns to the blood, osmolarity falls back towards normal. The osmoreceptors swell back, their signals weaken, and less ADH is released. That's negative feedback: a rise in concentration led to a response that lowers it. ADH release varies with concentration and can become extremely low after a large water intake.

Now the litre of water. It's absorbed into the blood, and osmolarity falls. Osmoreceptors detect the dilution, and ADH release drops. Aquaporins are taken back out of the duct membrane, so less water can leave the duct. More water stays in the filtrate, and you make a large volume of pale, dilute urine until concentration is back in range. Same loop, opposite direction.

One more hormone often turns up beside ADH. Aldosterone, from the adrenal glands on top of the kidneys, responds mainly to low blood volume or pressure, such as after heavy fluid loss. It makes the later parts of the nephron reabsorb more sodium. When water channels are present, water follows the sodium by osmosis, helping restore blood volume. Aldosterone doesn't move water directly. ADH changes how much water can leave the duct, and aldosterone changes how much salt is taken back.
To keep them apart: ADH is the anti-wee hormone. Diuresis means making urine, so antidiuretic means less of it. And for aldosterone, water follows salt.

Two exam questions. First. A student eats a large packet of salted chips and drinks nothing for the next two hours. The salt is absorbed into the blood. Predict how ADH release and the student's urine will change. Then explain how this response limits further water loss, and why drinking water would help restore blood osmolarity. Pause here to answer.

The absorbed salt raises blood osmolarity, even without sweating. Osmoreceptors detect it, and the posterior pituitary releases more ADH. More aquaporins let the collecting ducts reabsorb more water, so you make less urine, and it's more concentrated. That limits further water loss. Drinking supplies new water to dilute the salt. The classic mistake is expecting ADH to make new water.

Second. On separate days, a healthy adult drank one litre of pure water, or one litre of a salt solution with the same concentration as their blood. The graph shows their urine output over three hours. Explain the urine output after drinking water, and explain why the salt solution caused little change. Pause here to answer.

Pure water diluted the blood, so ADH release dropped. With fewer aquaporins, less water was reabsorbed, so urine output peaked at about an hour, then fell as concentration recovered. The salt solution matched blood concentration, so osmolarity barely changed and ADH stayed about the same. The classic mistake is saying the kidneys respond to how much you drink: both drinks were one litre.

So for any water balance question, ask what happened to blood concentration, which way ADH moved, and what that did to the collecting ducts and the urine. Next, plants face the same problem without kidneys: how do they keep enough water?
